extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed inventions satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101: (1) whether the claim falls within one of the four statutory categories and (2) whether the claim is not directed to a judicial exception unless it includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more. Covers claim construction, Alice/Mayo two-part test, and procedures for rejections/analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories requirement (35 U.S.C. 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories. 35 U.S.C. 101 defines the four categories of invention: processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The latter three categories define 'things' or 'products' (must exist in some physical or tangible form for those categories) while the first category defines 'actions' (a series of steps or acts). See MPEP § 2106.03 for detailed information. It is not necessary to identify a single category so long as the claim falls into at least one. Non-limiting examples of claims not directed to any statutory category include information/data per se, software/computer program per se when claimed as a product without structural recitations, and transitory signal transmissions. If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions and 'significantly more' requirement (Alice/Mayo framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, the claimed invention also must qualify as patent-eligible subject matter, i.e., the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception. The judicial exceptions are abstract ideas, laws of nature and natural phenomena (including products of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Alice/Mayo two-part test: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon); (2) if so, determine whether additional elements individually or in combination amount to significantly more (the search for an 'inventive concept'). Integration of an exception into a practical application or an improvement in technology can render claims eligible. See MPEP §§ 2106.04 and 2106.05 for detailed guidance and controlling case law (Alice, Mayo, Diehr, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole prior to examining a claim for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI sets the boundaries of coverage sought by the claim and influences whether the claim covers subject matter beyond the four statutory categories or encompasses exceptions. Claim construction affects whether a claim is to a statutory category and whether it is directed to a judicial exception. If the BRI encompasses non-statutory embodiments (e.g., carrier waves), the claim may fail Step 1. Examiners should point out the BRI and may recommend amendment to narrow the claim if appropriate. See MPEP § 2111 for more on determining BRI; cases such as Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish illustrate how interpretation affects eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 (Eligibility Step 1) — whether claim is to a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole is to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-process categories verify the claim recites physical or tangible form. Examples and clarifying definitions: machine = concrete thing consisting of parts or devices; manufacture = tangible article given new form, quality, property or combination; composition of matter = combination of two or more substances. If the claim's BRI covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim fails Step 1. Best practice: recommend amendments to narrow claims to statutory embodiments where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A (Eligibility Step 2A) — whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (a judicial exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider abstract idea groupings (e.g., mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes), 'tentative abstract ideas', laws of nature, natural phenomena, and product-of-nature issues. Use doctrinal analyses such as 'markedly different characteristics' and consider whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application. See MPEP § 2106.04 and its subparts for examples and explanatory tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B (Eligibility Step 2B) — whether claim amounts to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether additional elements, individually or as an ordered combination, add significantly more than the exception (i.e., provide an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the additional elements effect an improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology; whether the claim is tied to a particular machine or transforms an article into a different state or thing (particular transformation); whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity (which weigh against eligibility); whether other meaningful limitations exist; beware of mere instructions to apply an exception or insignificant extra-solution activity. See MPEP § 2106.05 and subparts (2106.05(a)-(h)) for detailed guidance, examples, and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three eligibility pathways (Pathway A/B/C) and when to apply streamlined analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use three pathways to reach eligibility conclusions: Pathway A (self-evident eligibility/streamlined), Pathway B (claim not directed to a judicial exception), Pathway C (claim directed to a judicial exception but recites significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pathway A: claims that fall within a statutory category and whose eligibility is self-evident may be found eligible using a streamlined analysis (see MPEP § 2106.06). Pathway B: claims to a statutory category that are not directed to a judicial exception are eligible without Step 2B. Pathway C: claims directed to an exception that recite additional limitations amounting to significantly more are eligible. If uncertain about applicability of a streamlined analysis, examiners are encouraged to conduct the full Alice/Mayo analysis. If not eligible under any pathway, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/tangible form requirement and examples of non-statutory product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For machine, manufacture, and composition of matter categories, eligible subject matter must exist in some physical or tangible form; claims to intangible collections of information or software 'detached from any medium' may not fall within statutory categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of non-statutory product claims: data per se, computer program per se (software per se) claimed without structural recitations, transitory signal transmissions (propagating electrical or electromagnetic signals), and expressly excluded items such as humans per se. A product claimed only as code or instructions detached from a medium lacks physical embodiment and is not in a statutory category. See Digitech, Nuijten, Microsoft v. AT&T, In re Ferguson for case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments — examiner practices
rubrics_metrics.description: If the BRI of a claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When this occurs, it is best practice for the examiner to (1) point out the BRI, (2) recommend an amendment that would narrow the claim to statutory embodiments if possible, and (3) apply appropriate rejection (use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 where Step 1: NO). Examples: machine-readable medium claims whose BRI includes carrier waves should be rejected. See Mentor Graphics v. EVE-USA, In re Nuijten for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation and other tests as evidentiary clues (not separate tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue to eligibility but should not be used as a separate test; it should be considered as part of the integration/significantly more determination in the Alice/Mayo analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, the pre-Alice 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' test and the 'special purpose computer' rationale are superseded or limited by more recent Supreme Court precedent. Examiners should treat such tests as evidentiary guidance when assessing whether a claim integrates an exception into a practical application or recites significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101 is a threshold test — apply other statutes (102, 103, 112) as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 101 is only a threshold inquiry; even if an invention qualifies under §101, it must still satisfy the other statutory requirements for patentability (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, and 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners are reminded to make a complete examination under 102 (novelty), 103 (nonobviousness), and 112 (written description/enablement/definiteness), as well as utility and other requirements. Use these statutes as additional tools to ensure the claim meets conditions for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis criteria (MPEP § 2106.06) — when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility may be found via a streamlined analysis when it is self-evident that the claim is not directed to a judicial exception or clearly integrates an exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamlined analysis is appropriate when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident or when the claim clearly improves technology or computer functionality. If eligibility is not self-evident, conduct full Alice/Mayo analysis. See MPEP § 2106.06(a)-(b) for details and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting rejections for lack of subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on how to properly formulate, support, and document 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections and how to evaluate applicant responses and clarify the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specified form paragraphs (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)(1)) when making a 101 rejection. When a claim fails Step 1, use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. Evaluate applicant responses under MPEP § 2106.07(b) and clarify the record per § 2106.07(c). Maintain clarity in the prosecution history regarding claim construction/BRI and the factual/legal bases for eligibility conclusions.
